summary: An April 1 RFC and a humorous one. It is a parody of the Internet standards process, written as if documenting how a Roman community standardizes protocols, with stages, document types and even intellectual property rules. It is informational, not a real standards process.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke document that pretends ancient Romans had rules for approving new ideas, copying how real internet rules are made. It was published on April Fools' Day.

questions: april fools rfc standards process parody
subtitle: A humorous parody of the IETF standards process reimagined as ancient Roman governance.

tldr.problem: The IETF standards process is complex and formal. This April 1st joke reimagines it as if ancient Roman society had used the same procedures and terminology to standardize protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents a fictional 'Roman Standards Process' with Latin terminology (Roman Standards, RFCs, Technical Specifications, Applicability Statements, standards tracks, and Worst Current Practice documents), mirroring real IETF process but with Roman flavor.
tldr.outcome: This playful parody highlights both the formality of real standards work and the absurdity of applying modern technical governance concepts to ancient civilizations.

today: RFC 2551 is an Informational RFC published on 1 April 1999, marked as 'Worst Current Practice' in the fictional sense. It remains unobsoleted and is celebrated as a clever parody that demonstrates both the complexity of real standards processes and the ability of technical communities to laugh at themselves.

sections.title: The Roman Standards Process
sections.content: This April 1st RFC is a parody of RFC 2026, the real IETF Standards Process document. It reimagines how an ancient Roman society would have governed technical standardization using the same process, terminology, and structure as the modern Internet standards body. The document is written entirely in mock-formal language, using Roman numerals for section numbers and referencing fictional Roman standards bodies like the Roman Architecture Board (RAB) and Roman Engineering Steering Group (RESG).
sections.plainLanguage: This is a joke that uses fancy Roman names and numbering to describe how ancient Romans might have approved new ideas the same way the Internet does it today.

sections.title: Roman Standards and Documents
sections.content: The RFC describes fictional 'Roman Standards' and introduces publication types that mirror real IETF documents. The 'Roman' network (a play on 'Internet') has its own RFC series, working groups, standards tracks with maturity levels, and a review process. It includes categories like Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, and Roman Standard, as well as Worst Current Practice (WCP) documents. The entire bureaucratic apparatus of the IETF is faithfully recreated in a Roman context.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke describes different types of official documents and approval levels, just like the real Internet standards process, but all named with Roman words and references.

sections.title: Standards Advancement and Process
sections.content: The document meticulously outlines a standards track with advancing maturity levels, conflict resolution procedures, variance processes, and intellectual property considerations. Working groups deliberate in open forums, specifications undergo multiple review cycles, and there are formal procedures for retiring obsolete standards. The RFC even addresses the complexity of incorporating external standards, much like modern standards bodies do, giving the process the full weight of formal governance even in its fictional context.
sections.plainLanguage: The document describes how an idea would be discussed, reviewed multiple times, approved, and eventually retired, with proper rules for who owns the ideas and how disputes are resolved.
